p: In the zinc and copper(II) sulfate reaction, each zinc atom **loses** two electrons and becomes a Zn²⁺ ion, and each Cu²⁺ ion **gains** two electrons and becomes a copper atom.
The electrons lost by zinc are exactly the electrons gained by copper(II) ions: one cannot happen without the other. That is why we speak of a **red**uction–**ox**idation (redox) reaction.

p: **Redox reaction:** a reaction involving the transfer of electrons.
**Oxidation:** the loss of electrons. **Reduction:** the gain of electrons.
**Oxidising agent:** a substance that accepts electrons. **Reducing agent:** a substance that donates electrons.
**The cross-over that costs marks.** The oxidising agent is itself **reduced**; the reducing agent is itself **oxidised**.
rules: **Zn** loses 2e⁻: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. It is **oxidised**, so it is the **reducing agent**.
**Cu²⁺** gains 2e⁻: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. It is **reduced**, so it is the **oxidising agent**.

screens.q: Three learners discuss Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.
choices: Ravi: Zinc is the oxidising agent, because zinc is oxidised.
Ravi has the cross-over wrong: zinc is oxidised, so zinc is the reducing agent.
Zoe: Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent: it takes electrons from the zinc, so it oxidises the zinc and is itself reduced.
An oxidising agent accepts electrons, so it is reduced.
Pieter: Copper is the oxidising agent, because copper is formed.
Pieter names a product: Cu is formed, but the agent is the reactant Cu²⁺.
screens.why: Zoe ✓. An oxidising agent accepts electrons, so it is reduced. Name the **reactant**, never the product, as the agent: Cu²⁺, not Cu.

screens.h: Worked example 27.1: magnesium and hydrochloric acid
screens.q: Magnesium ribbon reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCℓ → MgCℓ₂ + H₂. (a) Write the equation in terms of the particles that react. (b) Which species is oxidised? (c) Identify the oxidising agent. (d) Why is this classified as a redox reaction?

lines.x: Mg + 2H⁺ + 2Cℓ⁻ → Mg²⁺ + 2Cℓ⁻ + H₂, so Mg + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂
Magnesium, Mg: it loses two electrons, Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.

choices: Mg
It loses two electrons: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.
H⁺
H⁺ gains electrons: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Gaining electrons is reduction.
Cℓ⁻
Cℓ⁻ is the same on both sides: it does not take part in the electron transfer.

lines.x: H⁺ (the hydrogen ions of the acid): they accept electrons, 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.

choices: H⁺
They accept electrons: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
H₂
H₂ is a product. The oxidising agent is the reactant that accepts electrons.
Mg
Mg donates electrons: it is the reducing agent.

lines.x: Electrons are transferred ✓: magnesium loses electrons (is oxidised) and H⁺ ions gain them (are reduced) ✓.

why: A learner writes “H₂ is the oxidising agent”. Explain the mistake.
H₂ is a product ✓. The oxidising agent is the reactant that accepts electrons: H⁺ ✓.

p: Table 4 on the data sheet is a list of **reduction** half-reactions. Each row has an oxidising agent (OA) on the left and the reducing agent (RA) it turns into on the right.
Oxidising agents get **stronger going down** (F₂ is the strongest); reducing agents get **stronger going up** (Li is the strongest).
The more **positive** E^{θ}, the stronger the oxidising agent on the left; the more **negative** E^{θ}, the stronger the reducing agent on the right.

choices: Fe³⁺
Fe³⁺ is twice on the left; its stronger row is +0,77 V, still weaker than +1,77 V.
Fe
Fe is only ever on the right, so it can never be an oxidising agent.
H₂O₂
H₂O₂ is on the left of the +1,77 V row.
I₂
I₂ (+0,54 V) is far weaker.
screens.why: H₂O₂ is on the left of the +1,77 V row. Do not use the +0,68 V row: there H₂O₂ is on the right, as a reducing agent.

screens.h: Turning a row into a half-reaction
p: A **reduction** is the row copied with a single arrow. An **oxidation** is the row written **backwards**, so the electrons end up on the right.
The E^{θ} value is never changed and never multiplied.

p: A half-reaction never happens alone: the electrons lost in the oxidation must all be gained in the reduction. So the two half-reactions are added, after multiplying one or both so that the numbers of electrons are equal.

ask.prompt: Add the two half-reactions. Which is the balanced overall equation?
choices: 2Aℓ + 3Ni²⁺ → 2Aℓ³⁺ + 3Ni
The 6e⁻ cancel. Charge: left 3(+2) = +6; right 2(+3) = +6.

The charges do not balance: +2 on the left, +3 on the right. Multiply first.
